paper.quote: Descending predictions include wall reflections; ascending predictions anticipate the earliest possible brick bounce and revise as the ball climbs.
paper.say: The game ends if the ball reaches the bottom row uncaught, so the paddle must get under it in time. The model says it predicts the landing spot, counting bounces off the side walls for a falling ball. For a rising ball, it assumes the earliest possible bounce off a brick and revises the prediction as the ball climbs.

check.note: Without sticky moves it catches all 1,064 reachable falling starts, all 872 rising starts under full bricks, and all 1,620 with no bricks above.

paper.quote: Early positioning favors preserving horizontal direction to sweep through bricks; near the bottom, either valid catch column is accepted.
paper.say: The model says that early on, the paddle favors a spot that keeps the ball going the same way sideways after the bounce, so the ball sweeps through the bricks and breaks them. Near the bottom, it accepts either column that still catches the falling ball.

check.note: 98.0% of 159,963 catches over 300 games kept direction, no stretch without a brick passed 175 steps, and all 102 either-cell late states stay still.

paper.quote: Units 0..3: descending-right, descending-left, ascending-right, ascending-left.
paper.say: On the board the ball is always flying diagonally, so it is going down-right, down-left, up-right or up-left. The model gives each of these cases its own unit, one small part of the network that outputs a number. Each unit works out where the paddle should go in that case.

check.note: All 306 ball entries across the four units decode to the true catch column, at 0.02 per column.

paper.quote: Subtract paddle position from each target.
paper.say: The paddle needs to know how far it is from the target, and in which direction. So the model has each of the four units also read the paddle's column in the bottom row and subtract it from the target. The result is the landing-position error, which tells the paddle how far off it is.

check.note: Paddle weights are exactly -0.02 per column on all four units, matching the 0.02 per column of the ball tables.

paper.quote: Ball row 6: descending targets become catch-interval midpoints.
paper.say: The model says near the bottom either of two columns can catch the ball. So from row 6 down, a falling ball's target becomes the midpoint of the catching columns. The paddle then aims for the middle of that range instead of one exact column.

check.note: 48 of 54 entries in rows 6 to 8 are half-column midpoints, and the other 6 are wall cells where both catch cells coincide.

paper.quote: Unit 4: horizontal direction, including stationary wall-reflection frames.
paper.say: The landing prediction depends on which way the ball is going sideways. One unit finds this by comparing the ball's column with its trail, the cell the ball just left. The model also covers the frames where the ball stays in one column while it reflects off a side wall.

check.note: Right on 99.8% of 232,568 frames and all 23,309 wall frames; all 409 misses are the single frame after a paddle hit reverses the ball.

paper.quote: Unit 5: descending versus ascending; a stationary row-8 frame means paddle bounce.
paper.say: The model also needs to know whether the ball is falling or rising. A second unit finds this by comparing the ball's row with its trail. If the ball stays in row 8, just above the paddle, for one frame, the model reads that as a bounce off the paddle.

check.note: Right on 99.6% of frames and all 17,975 paused row-8 frames; the 1,039 misses are pauses in rows 0 to 2 after the ball hits a brick from above.

paper.quote: Four context-gated pairs of left/right comparisons.
paper.say: The second layer of the network holds four pairs of left and right comparisons, one pair for each way the ball can be flying. The two direction units select the pair that matches the ball's real flight. So the paddle follows the prediction that fits what the ball is doing.

check.note: Never more than one of the 8 units fires, and it belongs to the true direction on 98.8% of moving frames; the rest are the one-frame misreads above.

paper.quote: Near-deterministic movement when needed; otherwise no-op.
paper.say: The network ends with a score for each move, and the game picks a move at random, favoring high scores. When the paddle needs to slide left or right to reach the ball, the model makes that score very high, so the move happens almost every time. When the paddle is already in the right place, it stays still.

check.note: The top action had over 90% probability on every one of 232,568 frames, with 50.7% still, 24.6% left and 24.7% right.

astra.quote: two valid landing cells, including wall reflections
astra.say: The model says it predicts the two cells where the paddle can catch the ball, so the paddle knows where to go. The prediction counts any bounces off the side walls on the way down.

check.note: Over all 1,440 falling states, all 1,168 that need a move get the right one, and 268 of 272 states already in place stay or take the optional step.

astra.quote: During ascent, it anticipates the earliest possible brick collision and revises that prediction when the ball passes through holes.
astra.say: A rising ball turns back when it hits a brick, so the landing spot depends on where that happens. The model plans for the earliest possible brick hit. If the ball passes through a hole in the bricks, it revises the prediction.

check.note: Without sticky moves it catches all 872 rising starts under full bricks and all 1,620 with no bricks, though it steers to the far cell in 132 of 148 such choices.

astra.quote: Movement is nearly deterministic, while safe final-step choices are randomized to avoid repetitive trajectories
astra.say: The model says the paddle's moves are almost fully determined by where the ball is, with one exception. On the final step before a catch, when more than one paddle choice is safe, the choice is left to chance. The aim is to stop the ball from repeating the same path over the bricks.

check.note: The coin flip is real, 50/50 on row 8 only, yet 31% of steps fall in stretches over 500 steps with no brick, and deleting it lifts 381 to 452 over 300 games.

astra.quote: Paddle coordinate in every landing comparison.
astra.say: To decide whether to slide left or right, the network must compare the paddle with the cell where the ball will come down. So the model has twenty comparison units read the paddle's column in the bottom row. A unit is one small switch in the network.

check.note: Weights are exactly -8 per column on units 0 to 19, and those units read fully on or off on over 99% of frames.

astra.quote: Horizontal direction, including zero-displacement wall reflections.
astra.say: The prediction needs to know which way the ball is going sideways. One unit finds this by comparing the ball's column with its trail, the cell the ball just left. The model also covers wall bounces, where the ball does not change column for a step.

check.note: Right on 96.5% of 272,546 frames and all 28,919 wall frames; all 9,637 misses are the single frame after a paddle hit reverses the ball.

astra.quote: Vertical direction: distinguish brick and paddle bounce plateaus.
astra.say: Another unit does the same with rows, to tell a rising ball from a falling one. The ball can stay in the same row for a step when it bounces. The model has this unit tell a bounce off a brick, after which the ball falls, from a bounce off the paddle, after which it rises.

check.note: Right on 99.1% of frames and all 17,828 paused row-8 frames; the 2,475 misses are pauses in rows 0 to 2 after the ball hits a brick from above.

astra.quote: Second-layer Boolean gates.
astra.say: The model says the second layer turns the comparisons into movement rules for the paddle. Each second-layer unit works like a logical AND. It switches on only when a comparison between the paddle and the ball's landing cell holds and the ball is flying in the matching direction.

check.note: Falling-flight units 0 to 5 match true falling on 89% of their 17,554 frames, rising units 6 to 11 on 100%, and optional units 12 to 17 fired only on row 8.

astra.quote: Prefer inward catch positions near the edges.
astra.say: When the ball will come down near a side wall, the model prefers the catch cell closer to the middle of the board. Two second-layer units add this preference, using the edge detectors from the first layer.

check.note: 98.7% of 17,021 edge catches used the inner cell; this is the main flaw, since 68 of 73 long stalls wait on a corner brick and removing it lifts 381 to 462.

astra.quote: Required moves dominate; optional safe moves tie with no-op.
astra.say: The network ends with a score for each move, and the game picks a move at random, favoring high scores. A move the paddle must make to reach the ball gets a score that beats everything else. An optional safe move gets the same score as staying still, so either one can happen.

check.note: Top action exceeded 90% on 95.8% of frames, and the other 4.2%, all on row 8, split 50/50 between staying and the optional move.

claude.quote: predicts where the ball will be when it reaches row 8 on its way down
claude.say: The model's plan needs only one prediction, namely where the ball will be when it reaches row 8 on its way down. Row 8 is the row just above the paddle. The paddle moves into position for that spot and waits there.

check.note: Over all 1,440 falling states the chosen action matches this rule exactly, and all 1,064 reachable starts are caught without sticky moves.

claude.quote: the ball is caught if the paddle ends that step at x8 or at x8+d8
claude.say: The model points out that the game moves the paddle first and the ball second. So when the ball is in row 8, the paddle can catch it from either of two cells. One is directly under the ball, and the other is one cell ahead in the ball's sideways direction.

check.note: A sweep of 600 row-8 cases through the game code agrees with this rule in all 600.

claude.quote: The 2-cell zone also makes the paddle tolerant of a sticky repeat when it arrives.
claude.say: The game sometimes repeats the player's last move by accident, which is called a sticky action. The model says having two good cells gives the paddle some tolerance for this. A sticky repeat just as the paddle arrives does not ruin the catch.

check.note: A forced repeat on the catch step dropped the ball 1 time in 4,232, against 11 in 306 for the paper's network; 3 of 80 deaths had one in the last 3 steps.

claude.quote: assume the earliest possible turn, at row min(4, r)
claude.say: The model assumes a rising ball turns back as early as it possibly could, at row 4, just below the bricks. Its reason is that this is the most urgent case, leaving the paddle the least time. If the ball goes higher, the prediction updates while time remains.

check.note: All 324 rising entries follow this formula and all 1,620 no-brick starts are caught, though row 1 wrongly assumes a brick above it, giving 68 wrong moves for one frame.

claude.quote: That makes them a lookup table, which is linear in the one-hot ball input.
claude.say: For a ball flying in a given direction, say down-right, the spot the paddle should reach depends only on which cell the ball is in now. So the model stores those paddle columns as a table, with one number for each ball cell. Exactly one ball cell is lit in the input, so a plain weighted sum reads the right entry.

check.note: All 612 entries in units 0 to 7 equal the simulated catch cell, and the units read fully on or off on nearly all frames.

claude.quote: with a wall correction for the case where the ball and trail share a column after a wall bounce
claude.say: The landing prediction depends on which way the ball is going sideways. Unit 8, one small switch in the network, compares the ball's column with its trail, the cell it just left. After a wall bounce the two can share a column, so the model adds a correction for that case.

check.note: Right on 98.1% of 252,220 frames and all 26,621 wall frames; all 4,817 misses are the single frame after a paddle hit reverses the ball.

claude.quote: It is +1 when the ball is ascending or level at row 8, and −1 when descending or level elsewhere.
claude.say: Unit 9 does the same with rows, to tell a rising ball from a falling one. The ball can stay level for a step when it bounces. The model reads this as a paddle bounce, so rising, if it happens in row 8, and as a ceiling or brick bounce, so falling, anywhere else.

check.note: Right on 98.4% of frames and all 17,336 paused row-8 frames; the 3,925 misses are pauses in rows 0 to 2 after the ball hits a brick from above.

claude.quote: Each unit is the AND of one comparison unit with its mode
claude.say: The first layer has a "go right" and a "go left" signal for the paddle in each of the ball's four flight directions. Each of the eight second-layer units switches on only when its signal says move and units 8 and 9 confirm the ball is flying that way. So the paddle follows only the prediction that fits the ball.

check.note: Never more than one unit fires on 252,220 frames, and it matches the true direction on 93.3% of moving frames, the rest being the one-frame misreads.

claude.quote: The no-op-like actions (n, u, d, f) stay at 0, so the paddle waits when it is in the zone.
claude.say: The network gives each move a score. The model keeps the four actions that leave the paddle in place at a score of 0, while left and right get +12 when the paddle must slide to reach the ball and −12 otherwise. So once the paddle is in the catching zone, it waits for the ball.

check.note: A firing unit puts its move at +12 against 0, and otherwise at -12, so 54% of frames wait across the four idle actions.

paper.quote: stay in column 5, approach nearby incoming treasure, and wait in its row.
paper.say: In this game enemies and gold treasure cross the board along rows, and touching an enemy ends the game. The model's cautious plan keeps the player in column 5. The player moves up or down toward nearby gold coming its way, and waits in that row for the gold to arrive.

check.note: Over 300 games it spent 100% of steps in column 5 and held still beside approaching gold in its row (1.00), though only 57% of the time on a quiet board.

paper.quote: Player-conditioned upward hazards.
paper.say: Before moving up, the player needs to know it will not step into an enemy crossing that row. So the model uses eight units, each one small switch in the network, that warn against moving up. Each combines the player's position with an enemy in the row above or two rows above, in case the game repeats the move by accident.

check.note: From row 5, an approaching enemy within 2 columns cuts the up score by 112 to 121 one row up and 61 to 112 two rows up, and a departing one cuts nothing.

paper.quote: Player-conditioned waiting hazards and edge-row penalties.
paper.say: Standing still can also be dangerous if an enemy is coming along the player's own row toward it. So another eight units warn when waiting in the current row is unsafe. The model also gives them extra penalties for the edge rows.

check.note: An approaching enemy in the player's row cuts the stay score by 121 at 1 column, 61 at 2 and 9.5 at 3, and an empty board always pushes the player out of rows 1 and 8.

paper.quote: Signed distance codes for treasure rows 1 through 8.
paper.say: To head for gold in another row, the player must know how far away that row is and in which direction. So the model gives each row a unit holding a signed code of the distance between the player and that row. The sign says whether the row is above or below.

check.note: With gold in row 3 and the player in row 5, unit 26 reads 1.4 before the gold passes, which is the written code for two rows up.

paper.quote: Trails cancel receding enemies and already-passed treasure.
paper.say: A player staying in column 5 can ignore an enemy or piece of gold that has already passed that column and is moving away. The trail, the cell just behind each object, shows which way it is moving. The model gives trail cells weights that cancel those objects, so they stop counting.

check.note: Across every column and direction of gold, the signal is 1.4 before it passes and -6.6 after, so passed gold leaves move choices at empty-board values.

paper.quote: Second-layer hazard aggregation.
paper.say: Enemies crossing the rows set off many warnings, and the model collects them into three second-layer units. One gathers the warnings about moving up, one about moving down, and one about staying put. This leaves one danger signal for each of these three choices.

check.note: One firing warning unit swings unit 0 from -0.76 to +0.75, and in play the chance of stepping beside an enemy 0 to 1 cells from the column was 0.005.

paper.quote: Treasure window decoders.
paper.say: A row's distance code is a single number, but the player must act differently when gold is level with it and when gold is above or below. The model's second-layer units split that number into windows. Each window answers one question, such as whether the gold is level with the player or some distance away.

check.note: Player in row 5: gold in rows 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 lights units 10-12, 14-16, 18-19, 22, 26. An empty board lights none of them.

paper.quote: Safety penalties.
paper.say: Touching an enemy ends the game, so the model makes each danger signal take 80 off the score of one choice, whether up, down or waiting. This large penalty is meant to stop the player from making a move flagged as dangerous.

check.note: The swing is 121 points, far above any treasure pull, yet 39% of 300 deaths came from a repeated move and 68% at top game speed.

paper.quote: Distance-decaying upward attraction.
paper.say: Gold above adds to the score for moving up, and the amount shrinks as the gold gets further away. Gold below does the same for moving down. This matches the plan of going for nearby gold.

check.note: From row 6 the chance of going up is 1.00, 1.00, 0.98, 0.88, 0.67 for gold 1 to 5 rows above, and 55 of 56 row pairs steer correctly.

astra.quote: I use a conservative central-column collector.
astra.say: The model calls its player a cautious collector that gathers gold from the central column. When avoiding enemies and collecting gold conflict, avoiding enemies comes first.

check.note: It spends 81% of steps in column 5, yet only 28% of 200 deaths happen there, and sideways moves are 11% of actions.

astra.quote: trails are conservatively ignored.
astra.say: The trail is the cell just behind each enemy or piece of gold, and it shows which way that object is moving. The model chooses not to use this information, and calls that choice conservative.

check.note: No weight reads the trail, and this is the main flaw: hiding departing enemies and gold from the input raises the score from 33.0 to 41.1 over 300 games. Without the trail cells the network cannot tell whether an enemy or gold piece is coming or going.

astra.quote: First layer: paired relative-horizontal enemy features, one pair per row.
astra.say: An enemy slides along its row, and the player needs to know where it is relative to the player. So the model gives each row a pair of units, each one small switch in the network. The two units of a pair compare the enemy's column with the player's column, one for each side.

check.note: Both units of a pair are positive when the enemy is within 1 column of the player, and they grade smoothly with column gap, as designed.

astra.quote: Treasure gates; absent treasure reproduces a player-row threshold.
astra.say: Eight units normally just record whether the player is below a certain row, which the model calls a player-row threshold. Gold crossing a unit's row changes the unit's value. That change tells the next layer which row has gold, and with no gold the unit is just the threshold.

check.note: Bug: gates are one-sided, so gold in rows 1-4 pulls only a player below it and rows 5-8 only a player above, leaving 12 of 56 row pairs with no pull.

astra.quote: Extreme row pairs share conservative hazard units.
astra.say: These second-layer units warn that moving left, moving right or staying still is unsafe because of an enemy near the player. Rows 1 and 2 share warning units, and so do rows 7 and 8. The model calls this sharing conservative, since an enemy in either row of a pair can trigger the warning.

check.note: Bug: any enemy in the player's row, at any distance or direction, sets staying to zero, which blocks it on 31% of steps at low speed and 68% at top speed.

astra.quote: Upward hazards: destination and possible repeated-action destination.
astra.say: Before moving up, the model checks the row the player would reach and also the row after it, because the game may repeat the move by accident. If an enemy threatens either place, these units mark moving up as unsafe.

check.note: From row 5 the chance of going up falls from 0.017 to 0.000 with an enemy within 1 column one row up or within 2 columns two rows up.

astra.quote: Horizontal recentering.
astra.say: The plan is to stay near the central column as enemies and gold cross it. So if the player is away from column 5, one unit reads how far and pushes the player back toward the middle.

check.note: Bug: the +18 pull works on an open board (0.999 from column 4), but when every move is blocked it picks the move, and 148 of 300 deaths were chosen sideways steps.

astra.quote: Treasure-directed vertical motion with central-row tie breaking.
astra.say: One unit adds up the gold signals from all rows and turns the total into a push up or down, so the player moves toward gold. Rows near the middle of the board count the most. The model uses this to settle ties in favor of the central rows.

check.note: It chases passed gold (0.41; paper 0.19, claude 0.11) and abandons awaited gold (stays 0.58; others 1.00), collecting 0.040 gold per step against 0.063.

astra.quote: Outputs: safety dominates navigation.
astra.say: The model says safety comes first. A warning takes far more off a move's score than the pull toward gold or the center can add. So a dangerous move loses, even if gold lies beyond it.

check.note: With gold in row 3 and an enemy at column 5 in row 4, the chance of going up from row 5 is 0.000, since a warning costs about 200 points and gold adds 12.

claude.quote: The player never moves left or right.
claude.say: The model's plan is that the player never moves left or right and stays in column 5, where it starts. Every enemy and piece of gold crosses its whole row, so each one passes column 5 at some point. The only decision left is which row to be in.

check.note: Over 300 games it spent 100% of steps in column 5, and left, right and fire score 20 below staying.

claude.quote: Each entity slot owns one row, so a row holds at most one entity.
claude.say: The model read the game's code and noticed that each row holds at most one enemy or piece of gold. So the row's single trail cell, the cell just behind that object, shows which way it is moving. This lets a simple weighted sum of a row's cells tell whether something is approaching.

check.note: True in the source: an entity's slot number sets its row and a slot holds one entity, so the row's trail cell always belongs to it.

claude.quote: P_r, units 0–7: player is in row r, for rows 1–8.
claude.say: Since only the choice of row matters, the network must first know which row the player is in. The model uses eight units, one for each of rows 1 to 8. A unit is one small switch in the network, and each of these outputs about +1 or −1.

check.note: Player in row 5: unit 4 reads +0.999 and the other seven read -0.999.

claude.say: To leave a row in time, the player must know how close an enemy is to column 5. Each row has a unit whose danger reading climbs as an approaching enemy gets closer, from −0.95 at five cells away up to 0.995 at column 5. An enemy moving away, an empty row or a row with gold counts as safe.

check.note: Measured 0.995, 0.964, 0.000, -0.537, -0.922, -0.947, and -0.964 for a departing enemy, all matching, with gold rows slightly lower at -0.999.

claude.quote: treasure in row s that is approaching column 5.
claude.say: The plan is to step into rows whose gold is heading toward column 5, then wait there. So each row has a unit that reads about +0.96 only when that row's gold is approaching. Otherwise it reads about −1.

check.note: Row 5: +0.964 for gold at every approaching position, -0.999 once it has passed, -0.964 for an empty row.

claude.quote: Each unit has weight 7 on P_r and a bias that includes −7.
claude.say: The second layer has one unit for "move up from row r" and one for "move down from row r". The model sets each unit to sit at exactly −1, fully off, unless the player is in row r. So only the rules for the player's current row have any effect.

check.note: Player in row 5 on an empty board: units 3 and 11 read -0.36 and -0.37, and the other twelve read -1.000.

claude.quote: This guards against a sticky repeat of the move.
claude.say: When weighing a step into another row, the model also subtracts a little for an enemy two rows away, in case the game repeats the move by accident. Gold in other rows adds to a move's value, and this pull shrinks the further away the row is.

check.note: An enemy two rows up lowers the up score from -4.4 to -7.9, yet 71% of 300 deaths still came from a repeated move.

claude.quote: logit(up) = 12·ΣUP + 72, and logit(down) = 12·ΣDN + 72.
claude.say: The player only moves between rows, so the scores for up and down decide its next step. The model sets the numbers so that the units for all the other rows cancel out. The score then comes only from the unit for the player's current row.

check.note: Measured up in row 1 and down in row 8 both score exactly -12, as stated.

claude.quote: Enemy in own row 1–2 cells away, adjacent row safe
claude.say: The model's table says what it expects the player to do. With an enemy one or two cells away and the next row safe, it flees, and it never enters a row with an enemy 0 to 2 cells from column 5. It moves toward approaching gold in the next row, and with nothing nearby it stays.

check.note: All four table rows match: flee +9.9 to +11.9, enter danger -11.5 to -12.0, adjacent gold +4.1, nothing nearby -4.4.

paper.quote: The policy stays at the starting column, firing left while changing rows to intercept divers and attack enemies.
paper.say: In this game a submarine shoots enemies, picks up divers and must return to the surface for oxygen. The model's plan keeps the submarine in its starting column, firing to the left. It changes rows only to reach divers and attack enemies.

check.note: Over 300 games (436,536 steps) it stayed in column 5 facing left on every step and fired on 79%.

paper.quote: First layer: player row indicators.
paper.say: Since the submarine only moves up and down, the network must always know how deep it is. The model uses nine units, one for each of rows 0 to 8. A unit is one small switch in the network, and each of these switches on when the submarine is in that row.

check.note: All nine units read the row correctly on 436,536 of 436,536 game states.

paper.quote: Diver presence in rows 2 through 8.
paper.say: The submarine must find divers to pick up. Seven units, one for each of rows 2 to 8, light up for a diver in that row. One input layer shows divers and enemies together, and another shows enemies, so each unit adds the first and subtracts the second to leave the divers.

check.note: No false alarms in 2.6 million row checks and 94.8% of diver rows caught; misses come from an enemy on the diver's cell or a bullet in the row.

paper.quote: Collision risk near the fixed player column.
paper.say: Enemy fish and enemy submarines cross the screen, and being hit ends the game. Since the submarine stays in one column, the model only watches around that column, with eight units, one per row, and the heaviest weights on columns 4 to 6. This marks which rows are risky to be in.

check.note: Lit for 99.95% of threats in column 5, 97% in columns 4 and 6, 12% of enemies in columns 3 and 7, and never on an empty row.

paper.quote: Left-side shooting opportunities in rows 2 through 8.
paper.say: The submarine fires to the left, so an enemy fish or enemy submarine on its left in the same row can be shot for a point. Seven units, one for each of rows 2 to 8, look for this in columns 0 to 3 of that row.

check.note: Matched the true state on all 3.06 million row checks; removing this pull in layer two cut the score from 50 to 24 over 400 games.

paper.quote: Second layer: fire candidate gated by current row.
paper.say: For each row the submarine could be in, the second layer has three options, namely stay and fire, go up, or go down. Only the options for the submarine's current row are switched on. Divers and shooting chances in other rows add to these options, and their pull fades with distance.

check.note: It stayed in a diver's row on 97% of steps and stepped toward a lone diver on 20% (up) to 33% (down) of steps; removing diver pull cut the score from 50 to 39.

paper.quote: Immediate destination hazards.
paper.say: If the row the submarine would end up in has an enemy near its column, every option that ends there gets a strong penalty. The model means this to keep the submarine from stepping into danger, whether it stays, goes up or goes down.

check.note: Only 0.16% of chosen vertical moves aimed at a row with an enemy near column 5, and removal cut the score from 50 to 2.8; 206 of 300 deaths were sticky repeats.

paper.quote: Oxygen-driven ascent, gated against empty surfacing.
paper.say: The submarine must surface for oxygen, but surfacing with no diver ends the game. So one unit asks for surfacing only when oxygen is below 60 and at least one diver is aboard, and that unit pushes all the up options. The model gives the last step to the surface its strongest push from this unit.

check.note: The request was right on all 436,536 states, up from row 1 with no diver was never chosen in 2,445 steps, and removing the climb cut the score to 4.3.

paper.quote: Action logits.
paper.say: The last layer turns the chosen option into a move of the submarine. Each fire option adds 30 to the score for fire, and each up or down option adds 30 to that move, with 40 for the last step to the surface. Left, right and doing nothing start at −100, which fits the plan of staying in one column.

check.note: On an empty screen the scores are fire 1.8, up and down 0, the rest -100; fire leads on 81% of steps, and the sampled move is the top one 95% of the time.

astra.quote: The policy holds a central firing position, seeks divers, then also targets enemies when the gauge suggests a passenger.
astra.say: The model's plan holds the submarine in a central firing position, and it goes after divers. It also goes after enemies when the gauge suggests a passenger, meaning a diver on board. The gauge is the pair of bars along the bottom that show oxygen and divers.

check.note: It sat in column 4 on 92% of 71,520 steps, but half of all steps were up or down moves and only 49% were shots.

astra.quote: Target detectors: divers first, enemies also when gauge permits
astra.say: Eight units, one per row, mark that row as a place to go. A unit is one small switch in the network. Each lights up for a diver in its row, and when a gauge cell on the diver bar is lit, an enemy in the row counts too.

check.note: Divers read at 98% and enemies at 89% with the cell lit, but cell (9,8) is also the top of the oxygen bar, so it was lit on 38% of diverless steps.

astra.quote: Threats in columns 2 through 7, gated by nearby player row
astra.say: The model wants the submarine to dodge nearby enemy fish, enemy submarines and enemy bullets. Eight units each watch one row for such danger in columns 2 to 7. Each one counts only when the submarine is in or near that row.

check.note: Matched all 572,160 row checks, but the wide window drives it off rows it could shoot along: narrowing it to columns 4 and 5 raised the score from 1.6 to 4.0.

astra.quote: Immediate threats on the occupied row
astra.say: Eight more units light up for danger very close by, in columns 3 to 6 of the submarine's own row. The model uses them to penalize firing at that moment, because it prefers escaping to shooting when a threat is immediate.

check.note: Matched all 572,160 row checks; in 742 such steps it never fired and moved up or down on 97%.

astra.quote: Return only when oxygen is below 60 and a passenger is confirmed
astra.say: Surfacing refills oxygen only with a diver on board, and surfacing with none ends the game. So one unit reads two gauge cells, and it asks the submarine to return only when they show oxygen below 60 and a confirmed diver.

check.note: Right on all 71,520 states; it chose up on 62% of the low-oxygen steps and 7 of 400 games ran out of oxygen.

astra.quote: Coarse horizontal escape preference
astra.say: The model also wants the submarine to have a way to escape sideways from enemies. One unit compares danger in columns 2 to 4 with danger in columns 5 to 7, and it gives a rough preference for moving left or right, away from the danger. The model calls this preference coarse.

check.note: The nudge is worth at most 8 on a base of -20, so up or down won on 97% of immediate-threat steps, and removing the path left the score at 1.5.

astra.quote: Target steering and matching target-activation units
astra.say: The model's plan picks the shallowest row that has a target, either a diver or an enemy it may attack. Pairs of units compare the submarine's depth with that row and steer the submarine up or down toward it.

check.note: With no threat lit it moved toward the shallowest target on all 16,362 steps and fired on arrival 99.95% of the time.

astra.quote: Vertical threat repulsion; bottom-row threats repel upward
astra.say: Nearby threats push the submarine up or down, away from danger, and threats at the bottom row push it upward. The model gives threats a weight of 120 and targets such as divers weights of 11 to 22. So a threat counts for much more than a target when a move is chosen.

check.note: The bug: push and target pull trade turns, so 66% of vertical moves reverse the last one, and 261 of 300 deaths come when a sticky repeat carries that bounce into danger.

astra.quote: Baselines include cancellation constants
astra.say: A threat unit that is off still outputs a constant value, and that would push the submarine around with no enemy near. So the model builds matching constants into each move's fixed starting score. These cancel the inactive units, so only real threats move the submarine.

check.note: On an empty screen fire scores 8.0, up and down 0.0, left and right -20; a lit target adds 22, so it fired on only 46% of steps with an enemy in line.

claude.quote: The strategy is to dive, line up vertically with the nearest cluster of targets, face the target in my row, and fire.
claude.say: The model's plan is for the submarine to dive and line up in height with the nearest cluster of targets, such as divers or enemies. It then turns to face the target in its row and fires.

check.note: The steps run as described, but the reward layer mixes fish and divers: 81% of aiming steps pointed at a diver, and only 15% of shots had an enemy in the row.

claude.quote: It avoids rows 0 and 1 otherwise, because a sticky "up" there with no diver ends the episode.
claude.say: Surfacing with no diver ends the game, and the game sometimes repeats the last move by accident. The model says a repeated "up" in rows 0 or 1 could cause exactly this. So it keeps the submarine out of those top rows unless it is surfacing on purpose.

check.note: Up from rows 1 and 2 was chosen on 22 of 21,476 steps, yet it spent 16.5% of steps idling in row 1, and 8 of 600 games ended surfacing empty.

claude.quote: Units for rows the submarine is not in saturate at exactly −1.
claude.say: The submarine's choices depend on what is in its own row, so the network should ignore the other rows. So each per-row unit, one small switch in the network, sits at exactly −1 unless the submarine is in that row. Adding up a group of 8 such units then gives −7 plus the value for the submarine's own row.

check.note: Off-row units stayed within 0.000002 of -1 across 75,467 game states.

claude.quote: The four one-entity values (±1.2, ±0.4) reveal f.
claude.say: To shoot an enemy, the submarine must be facing it. The model gets the facing from one number that mixes the submarine's facing with the direction the enemy or diver in its row is moving. With one such object in the row, this number has four possible values, and these reveal the facing.

check.note: 99.4% of 26,103 one-object rows landed on the four predicted values (0.38 and 0.83, either sign, after the unit's squashing).

claude.quote: The value is tanh(s − c_e − f/2), which is positive when the entity is to the submarine's left.
claude.say: The submarine must also know which way to turn to face the enemy or diver in its row. So a second group of units, one per row, compares the submarine's column with that object's column. The result is positive when the object is to the submarine's left.

check.note: Side read correctly on 35,947 of 35,947 one-object states.

claude.quote: V also gets +12 for each enemy bullet in the submarine's row (−12 in row 8, so it dodges upward there).
claude.say: A third group of units steers the submarine by counting targets below minus targets above, with the next row counting double. An enemy bullet in the submarine's row adds 12 to that count, pushing it down out of the bullet's way. In row 8, the deepest it can go, the sign flips so it dodges upward.

check.note: The pull matched on 99.6% and it followed on 93%, but the dodge fired on 77% of 451 bullet states, and bullets caused 107 of 300 deaths.

claude.quote: Unit 24 is SURF (diver bar cell (9,8) lit and oxygen cell (9,1) dark, i.e. a diver on board and oxygen below 40).
claude.say: Oxygen runs down, and surfacing refills it only with a diver on board. So the model wants the submarine to surface when oxygen is low, if it carries a diver. One unit detects this from a lit cell on the diver bar and a dark cell on the oxygen bar, meaning a diver on board and oxygen below 40.

check.note: Correct on all 75,467 states and up was chosen on all 839 such steps; games last only 126 steps on average, so this ran 0.27 times per game.

claude.quote: three cuts A, B and C, which give facing-right = A − B + C.
claude.say: The submarine's facing is hidden in the combined row number from the first layer. The second layer tests that number against three thresholds and combines the results to read off whether the submarine faces right. This tells it whether it must turn toward the enemy or diver in its row.

check.note: Facing was right on 99.1% of 36,217 one-object states and on only 35% of 2,394 two-object states, since a second object swamps the sum.

claude.quote: Priorities: surfacing beats dodging, which beats aiming, which beats idle fire.
claude.say: Several moves can look right at once, so the model orders them by score size. Surfacing for oxygen beats dodging a bullet, dodging beats turning to aim at something in the submarine's row, and aiming beats firing by default.

check.note: The scores follow that order (28, 12, 8, 4), but nothing checks the next cell: 196 of 300 deaths stepped onto an enemy, 73 of them by turning.
